query: For a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy used as a thin coating on a conventional metal substrate, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs overall wear resistance and microscopic deformation during sliding in the intended high-temperature operating regime? Define a controlled change relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the corresponding directional changes in wear and deformation, state the regime in which those predictions should hold, identify supporting prior evidence, and specify a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the effective surface Cu segregation in the FeNiCrCoCu coating promotes the in situ formation of a continuous, Cu-rich oxide layer during high-temperature sliding that acts as a solid lubricant and mitigates subsurface dislocation activity, thereby reducing overall wear and microscopic deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: A FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy thin coating on a conventional metal substrate with a homogeneous elemental distribution and no intentional surface Cu enrichment.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled post-deposition heat treatment (or similar processing step) designed to drive Cu segregation toward the coating surface, relative to the baseline unmodified coating.
generation.conditions: High-temperature sliding regime (e.g., operating at 600–700°C) where oxidation kinetics are active but scale spallation remains limited.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of a continuous, Cu-rich oxide layer at the coating surface with an associated reduction of subsurface dislocation density.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the enhanced Cu at the surface preferentially oxidizes to form a lubricious oxide scale. This protective film reduces direct asperity contact and limits severe plastic deformation (e.g., dislocation generation and microcracking) in the subsurface during sliding.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline coating, the treated coating will exhibit lower wear rates (as indicated by reduced material loss) and a lower density of deformation-related microstructural defects in the subsurface after sliding tests.
generation.baseline: The as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating that lacks the enhanced surface Cu segregation and thus does not form a well-developed Cu-rich oxide layer under identical high-temperature sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate in regimes where temperature is sufficiently high (around 600–700°C) to enable oxidation but low enough to prevent excessive oxide scale spallation; outside this window either minimal oxidation or aggressive scaling may obscure the effect.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of Cu in forming lubricious oxide layers is plausible, the exact oxidation kinetics, continuity and thickness of the Cu-rich oxide, and its precise relation to subsurface dislocation dynamics remain to be quantitatively established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings: one set undergoes a controlled post-deposition heat treatment designed to promote Cu segregation while the other set remains as-deposited. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature sliding wear tests (e.g., in a pin-on-disk apparatus at ~650°C).
measurements: Wear rate quantified by mass loss and surface profilometry
Subsurface microstructure via transmission electron microscopy (e.g., dislocation density)
Surface oxide composition and continuity analyzed by X-ray Photoelectron Spectroscopy (XPS) or Energy Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the processed (Cu-enriched) coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in wear rate and subsurface deformation compared to the baseline, or if surface analysis fails to detect a continuous Cu-rich oxide layer, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: This paper utilizes in situ X-ray diffraction (XRD) to investigate the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). We found that (1) Mn is the major oxide-forming element in both vacuum and air environments, leading to the formation of non-protective oxides that deplete the bulk alloy of Mn; (2) no oxides like Cr 2 O 3 , Fe 2 O 3 , or Fe 3 O 4 were observed during the high-temperature oxidation behaviour of CrMnFeCoNi, which contradicts some previous studies on the isothermal oxidation of CrMnFeCoNi HEA. We also analysed and compared the experimental results with thermodynamic calculations by using ThermoCalc version 2022b software following the CALPHAD method. ThermoCalc predicted spinel oxide in a vacuum environment, along with halite oxides observed in experimental results; also, in an atmospheric environment, it predicted only spinel, indicating the need for further investigation into factors to validate the thermodynamic predictions. Abstract Conventional material processing approaches often achieve strengthening of materials at the cost of reduced ductility. Here, we show that high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment can help overcome the strength-ductility trade-off in structural materials. We report an initially strong-yet-brittle eutectic high entropy alloy simultaneously doubling its strength to 1150 MPa and its tensile ductility to 36% after the HPHT treatment. Such strength-ductility synergy is attributed to the HPHT-induced formation of a hierarchically patterned microstructure with coherent interfaces, which promotes multiple deformation mechanisms, including dislocations, stacking faults, microbands and deformation twins, at multiple length scales. More importantly, the HPHT-induced microstructure helps relieve stress concentration at the interfaces, thereby arresting interfacial cracking commonly observed in traditional eutectic high entropy alloys. These findings suggest a new direction of research in employing HPHT techniques to help develop next generation structural materials. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Mechanical properties, Mechanical engineering
